#318. Emma Heming Willis shares family photos as daughter Mabel turns 11

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage shows the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore

Heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”

In February, Willis’ family announced that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

#317. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: Lighter, brighter, but the touchscreen doesn't add much

It’s a notable evolution of the MacBook Pro at a much higher price.

The least interesting thing about Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro is the touchscreen. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, as it's awkwardly called, is better seen as a total redesign of Apple's premium laptops. Both models are slimmer and lighter on every front: The 14-inch model weighs 3 pounds, down from the standard MacBook Pro's 3.7 pounds, while the 16-inch model goes from 4.7 pounds to 4 pounds. It also marks the first time the MacBook Pro has been graced with OLED screens, which are gloriously colorful in all the ways OLEDs tend to be.

Oh yeah, these new machines are also significantly more expensive. The 14-inch starts at $2,899, $900 more than the standard MacBook Pro. The 16-inch PROLED model will cost you $400 more than the regular version at $3,399.

In a time when computers already cost more, thanks to the AI-driven price increases for RAM, storage and other components, it seems odd for Apple to unleash its most expensive laptops yet. But I'm sure there's a crowd who will pay anything to have the sleekest MacBook Pro around. I just hope that Apple keeps its non-touchscreen MacBook Pros around for a long time (and maybe even brings those prices back down).

As you can tell from their name (which really should be something along the lines of the MacBook Pro Ultra), the PROLED XDR screen is the real selling point of these computers. And, at the very least, the display is impressive enough for Apple to create an entirely new marketing buzzword. Both the 14-inch and 16-inch revamped MacBook Pros have OLED screens that are slightly larger than the standard models (14.2-inches and 16.3-inches), which, together with thinner bezels, makes them feel a bit more immersive. They can reach up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR and 1,000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, making them the brightest OLED screens we've ever seen in laptops. They also sport an insanely high 10,000,000 to 1 contrast ratio.

Being OLED displays, where every pixel is turned on and off individually, they can reach pure deep blacks right alongside very bright elements. As someone who spent hundreds of hours staring at Apple's previous Mini LED-equipped MacBook Pros, which were already incredibly bright, I found it a bit hard to see the difference between the two screen technologies during normal usage. But when I was watching a movie with a dark background, which occasionally erupted into a bright scene, the PROLED XDR MacBook Pros looked more realistic. Watching the final scenes of F1: The Movie, where fireworks erupt against-black night sky for several minutes, felt absolutely revelatory on these screens.

The MacBook Pros with PROLED XDR also sport a Dynamic Island at the top of their screens, which houses their webcams and serves as a new home base for Spotlight and Live Activities. In practice, it works just like the Dynamic Island on iPhones — the displays morph around the black oval to reshape it for various tasks. It's slightly less noticeable than the notch on the standard MacBook Pros, but it ultimately doesn't make a huge visual difference.

For all of the attention Apple paid to its new OLED screens and thinner design, it's surprising that the company has taken a very basic approach to bringing touchscreen support to macOS. The PROLED XDR touchscreens work as you'd expect: You can swipe on the screen to scroll through articles or manipulate 3D objects or other media. Touch interactions just register as mouse clicks, so you can use it for everything in macOS, and Apple also has plenty of creative application partners like Adobe and BlackMagic who plan to fully support the touchscreen. There's no Apple Pencil support, though, so if you actually want to draw you'll still need an iPad.

Both PROLED XDR MacBook Pros look almost the same as the standard models, but there are plenty of hidden refinements that have led to a significant weight reduction. The 3-pound 14-inch model feels closer to a MacBook Air than a MacBook Pro, while the 16-inch MacBook Pro now feels more like the standard 14-inch model, which weighs between 3.4 and 3.6 pounds. Apple was able to shave off the fractional pounds by moving to the lighter OLED displays, as well as reworking the MacBook Pro's cooling design and internal components. I don't have a huge problem with the weight of the standard MacBook Pros, but given that PC competitors are aggressively making their machines lighter, it's nice to see Apple following along.

Beyond the screen and a new case design, the PROLED XDR MacBook Pros also feature a slightly redesigned audio system with six speakers. Apple already had the best speakers I've ever heard in a laptop, and now they're just better with enhanced low end for boomy bass. I was able to crank up the 14-inch model while playing music in my backyard, and there was no distortion or loss of clarity. It simply sounded great as I tried to fill my neighborhood with the sounds of Jungle's Tiny Desk concert.

Under the hood, Apple's new MacBook Pros are running the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the previous models, so there shouldn't be any performance differences. Nothing has changed with the keyboard or trackpad either, but given that they're among the best we have already, I'm not complaining. Thankfully, Apple didn't make the same sacrifices as it did with the slim TouchBar MacBook Pros a decade ago. These PROLED XDR models all have the same ports as the standard MacBook Pros, including three USB-C Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, a headphone jack, a MagSafe power adapter and a full-size SD card slot.

Even without opening up these MacBook Pros, it's obvious that they're more refined. You can immediately feel how much lighter they are than before. And once you get working, the slightly bigger screens and the ability to just touch them whenever you want becomes wonderfully convenient. None of the upgrades are compelling enough to throw out your MacBook Pro if you have a recent M-series model, but they're nice to have if you're willing to pay a premium.

I'll reiterate, though, that the actual touchscreens from these systems aren't anything special. It's nice being able to casually scroll through the web and documents like I can on most Windows PCs, but it's not exactly a game changer. Games like Angry Birds Reloaded and Powerwash Simulator also work seamlessly with the touchscreen, though there are occasional issues, like not being able to trigger specific Angry Bird powers. Powerwash Simulator was also much more accurate using the MacBook Pro's touchpad (I'd wager it's just not optimized fully for touchscreens yet).

While we've had Windows laptops that can twist and turn in all directions to make better use of their touchscreens, Apple has avoided doing anything too crazy with these MacBook Pros. The hinges are a bit more stiff to withstand you touching the screen, but that's about it. If you want a touchscreen Apple device that can move between laptop and tablet modes, you'll still need to get an iPad with a keyboard case. There were rumors that the company was working on some sort of "hybrid" touchscreen interface for macOS, but there's no sign of that here.

Maybe Apple didn't call these systems "MacBook Pro Ultra" because they're basically just MacBook Pros with nicer screens and slimmer cases. They're not exactly changing any computing paradigms. And given that these models are running existing Apple chips, their benchmark performance also comes as no surprise. Our 14-inch review unit, which featured an M5 Pro chip and 48GB of RAM, delivered a single-core Geekbench 6 score of 4,217 points, in line with what we've seen from the rest of the M5 family. That single-core figure is one of the highest we've seen this year, bested only by the ridiculously powerful Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra chip and the MacBook Pro with an M5 Max.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lasted around 12 and a half hours on my workflow, which mostly involves juggling tons of browser tabs, Slacking, image editing, writing, video chatting and occasionally taking some video breaks. Apple claims the 16-inch model can get up to 24 hours of runtime with light web browsing and 1080p video streaming. In my testing, the 16-inch PROLED MacBook Pro lasted for 10 hours and 15 minutes while running a benchmark script replicating real-world coding work.

Given the huge price jump, these aren't systems I can easily recommend to casual buyers. If you're a professional who demands the best quality screen available, or if you travel a lot, it may be worth the significant premium for a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro. At the moment, the 16-inch model seems like the better value, since it's only $400 more than the standard 16-inch MacBook Pro. Spending $900 more just to get a touchscreen OLED 14-inch MacBook Pro just doesn't make much sense, unless you're aiming to get the lightest MacBook Pro possible.

It's hard not to look at the MacBook Pros with PROLED XDR Displays and avoid getting angry about skyrocketing hardware prices. Earlier this year, the 14-inch MacBook Pro started at $1,699, while the 16-inch model went for $2,699. But the price hikes in June pushed them up to $1,999 and $2,999, respectively. Now, Apple is pushing its lineup even higher just for a redesign and better screen.

The obscene prices are unfortunate, but if you're eager to get your hands on the best MacBook Pros around, you'll have to suffer through them. Maybe Apple will actually lower its prices in a few years once RAM and SSD demand stabilizes, but by that point you can likely also save a ton from buying a used or refurbished model. At these price levels, we'll have to start thinking about buying computers like we do cars, where it rarely makes sense to buy something new.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Displays isn't exactly revolutionary for Apple, but it shows there's still plenty of room for the company to refine its designs even further. Both the 14-inch and 16-inch models feature OLED screens that are so beautiful to watch, you won't notice that the actual touchscreen experience is fairly basic. If you've already spent a ton on a recent standard MacBook Pro, though, there's no need to rush out and upgrade. Those systems still have great screens and they perform just as fast.

#316. 2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini

It’s more compelling than ever, but also more expensive.

The iPad mini has long felt like a niche product. It has earned a reputation as a quality tablet for people who want something small, comfortable, and portable, but its small screen and comparatively limited processing power have restricted its appeal, making it best suited to watching media or playing games.

With the 2026 version, the iPad mini is more competitive than ever. Its chip is current, its speakers are better, and, most impressively, it trades its 8.3-inch IPS screen for an 8.5-inch OLED that can hold its own against other premium tablets. There isn’t much more you can ask of an iPad this small.

But at just $50 less than the larger, more powerful iPad Air (11-inch), the iPad mini still has a hard time making a case for itself.

The most immediately noticeable change to the 2026 iPad mini is its display. At 0.2 inches larger than the 2024 iPad mini’s screen, the difference might not sound like much, but it has a meaningful impact on a tablet this small. Beyond providing a bigger view of photos, video content, and lengthy documents, the extra space makes it easier to work with multiple windows, giving you more room to view them and adjust their size and location.

One of our biggest complaints about the prior mini was its bezels, which felt large for a tablet of its size. This time, Apple managed to fit a larger screen in a slightly smaller tablet (7.69 × 5.22 × 0.21 inches and 0.56 pounds for the 2026 mini versus 7.69 × 5.3 × 0.25 inches and 0.65 pounds for the 2024 mini) by reducing the bezels by 24 percent. The result is a streamlined viewing experience that feels more modern and appropriate for a new Apple product.

And you’ll certainly want to watch content on the 2316 × 1512 OLED display, which packs 326 pixels per inch. OLED displays often lack the brightness of their LCD-LED counterparts, but the gap has narrowed in recent years. The new mini is brighter than its IPS-based predecessor, with Apple claiming full-screen brightness of up to 600 nits, compared to 500 nits on the previous model. It’s also much better suited to HDR content, with peak HDR brightness reaching 1,200 nits for highlights and a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1.

Since content consumption is arguably the mini’s strongest use case, it makes sense for Apple to focus on changes that enhance the viewing experience. Watching shows and movies feels as luxurious as possible on a screen this size, and the mini maximizes its display in nearly all the ways that matter.

I say “nearly” because the mini still has a 60 Hz refresh rate; 120Hz is limited to the iPad Pro. A 120 Hz refresh rate makes little difference when watching most shows or movies, but it can make some tasks, such as scrolling through long documents, look smoother. Still, the difference is less noticeable on a smaller screen.

Overall, the refresh rate didn’t feel like a drawback during regular use. Apple has gone a step further, noting that OLEDs typically have faster response times than IPS displays. That’s generally true when discussing gray-to-gray (GtG) response times. However, moving picture response time (MPRT) can be a better indicator of potential persistence-related motion blur, including during scrolling, because it measures how long an image remains visible on the display, contributing to blur as your eyes track moving content. GtG, by contrast, measures how quickly individual pixels transition between shades. Slower pixel transitions can create motion artifacts such as ghosting.

According to Blur Busters’ MPRT Indicator, the mini has an MPRT of about 17 ms, about what I’d expect from a 60 Hz IPS display. Anyone who needs a high-refresh screen will still want to look at the Pro series.

One feature the mini borrows from the iPad Pro but that other iPads lack is the option for nano-texture glass, which is designed to reduce glare. It costs an extra $100 and is only available on the 256GB and 512GB versions of the mini.

The 2024 mini debuted with a year-old chip, but this year’s model sports Apple’s latest mobile processor. The 2026 mini makes a considerable jump from the A17 Pro, a 3-nanometer, iPhone 15 Pro-era chip from 2023, to the A20 Pro, a 2-nanometer chip that debuted in the new iPhone 18 Pro.

The newer chip has 50 percent more memory bandwidth, which significantly boosts graphics performance. It’s also up to 60 percent faster.

I tested the 512GB version of the iPad Mini, which, like the 128GB and 256GB versions, features a seven-core integrated GPU. The 512GB model, however, gets a bump from five CPU cores to six and doubles the number of 16-core Neural Engines from one to two, promising better performance in on-device AI applications, such as image generation.

I don’t expect many people to run particularly intensive workloads on a tablet this small. Still, tasks such as photo editing, light video editing, and juggling many open applications felt smooth. The performance boost makes the iPad mini much more powerful than the standard iPad 11, which uses an A16 processor. The iPad Pro (M5) and the iPad Air (M4), however, remain better equipped for demanding workloads such as video editing and 3D rendering.

Siri AI is still in beta, so we won’t cover that in this review. But the tablet supports features under the Apple Intelligence umbrella, including various generative AI capabilities. Tasks like removing objects from photos, changing a photo’s perspective, or extending a photo’s borders should take roughly the same amount of time on the 512GB iPad mini as they do on the iPhone 18 Pro. In my experience, that’s usually about 20 seconds.

The mini is surprisingly loud. Its speakers are powerful enough to make TV dialogue easy to hear, even with my noisy heater running in the background.

The tablet has two woofers designed to deliver higher volume and stronger bass than the prior mini. A pair of custom-designed tweeters between the tablet’s glass and aluminum enclosure are intended to improve the clarity of higher frequencies.

You won’t get the deepest bass or the crispest high notes, but the speakers surpassed my expectations when playing music. I didn’t immediately feel the need to connect the iPad to dedicated speakers.

And the mini pulls this off without any visible speaker holes in its chassis.

That detail helped the mini earn the first IP67 rating for an iPad. The Ingress Protection rating means the device is “dust-tight” and “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water,” according to the International Electrotechnical Commission.

The 2026 mini has the same 12 MP front and back cameras as its 2024 predecessor, but the front-facing camera has moved from one of the shorter sides to one of the longer sides. This took some getting used to for FaceTiming and selfies. Holding the tablet in portrait orientation now places you off-center in the frame, while holding it in landscape mode to FaceTime on the go quickly became uncomfortable. The new location was fine when I could sit down and prop the tablet on a stand.

Another addition is the back camera’s Adaptive True Tone flash, which Apple markets as a way to quickly scan documents. When the Camera app identifies a document, such as a piece of paper or a book, it automatically adjusts which of the camera’s LEDs light up to minimize shadows and produce clearer text.

When I used the tablet’s camera to photograph text on both a piece of paper and a book, it quickly used machine learning to identify them as documents. A pop-up appeared, offering the option to “Scan Document”; selecting it allowed me to automatically take a picture of just the document. It’s not a feature many people will use regularly, but when the need arises, it makes capturing a sharp, detailed image of text considerably easier.

Additional upgrades include a move from Wi-Fi 6E to Wi-Fi 7 and from Bluetooth 5.3 to Bluetooth 6. These capabilities come from the introduction of Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, which also adds Thread support. Apple launched the N1 last year with the iPhone 17-series and iPhone Air.

The iPad mini also has the C2 cellular modem that Apple unveiled last month in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. For those who rely on cellular service, it’s reassuring that the tablet uses the same technology here as some of Apple’s best phones.

Although it’s not an upgrade, it’s impressive that the new mini has the same battery life as its predecessor, despite having a smaller chassis and a larger screen. The mini also gains support for fast charging.

With the 2026 model, the iPad mini feels less like a compromise. Its larger OLED screen, current-generation processor, more durable build, and better speakers make it feel more modern and competitive than the 2024 version.

These improvements come with a pricing predicament, though. Today, the iPad mini starts at $699 for the 128GB version, putting it just $50 below the 11-inch iPad Air (M4) at its lowest configuration. The 512GB mini I tested, which came with a more powerful A20 Pro chip, is $999. In 2024, the iPad mini started at $499, and the iPad Air 11-inch (M2) started at $599.

The mini’s OLED screen is a standout, but the Air remains a better choice for those seeking a balance between power and portability. Its more capable processor and still-excellent, larger IPS display make it more versatile. It also offers comparable battery life, though it lacks fast charging. Meanwhile, the Pro series remains the best option for demanding workloads and extensive multitasking. The Mini is much more capable of handling serious work, multitasking, and editing than it was before, but it still isn’t the best iPad for these purposes.

Despite narrowing the gap with other tablets, the mini is still a niche product. The biggest reason to pick it over other iPads is if you truly want the smallest device, primarily for content consumption. My preference for devices that are easy to handle without straining my smaller hands or weighing me down, combined with my appreciation of high-end displays, love of streaming, and interest in using secondary screens to boost productivity, confirms that this niche has an audience. Many of Apple’s improvements make the mini more enjoyable for these users.

Beyond comparisons with the rest of the iPad lineup, though, the mini makes the most of its small design. Apple fit just about everything it could into a device that’s somehow even smaller than its predecessor.

For anyone looking for an ultraportable tablet primarily for enjoying content on an excellent, high-end display, the mini is a markedly better device than it used to be.

With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#315. Apple iMac M6 review: Faster, more expensive and deeply in need of a refresh

Most buyers would be better off with a Mac mini and a bigger external display.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

With its new iPhone Duo and MacBook Pro touchscreen models, Apple is finally embracing change and shaking up its product mix. Unfortunately the new iMac M6 all-in-one — once one of Apple's most revolutionary products — has not been a beneficiary of that new ethos.

It is faster than ever thanks to the new M6 chip and updated memory. But the design, which hasn't changed since the 2021 iMac M1, is getting stale. The 24-inch display's small size is more of an issue than ever, considering that 27- and 32-inch monitors are now the norm. It's still a solid computer for consumers or business users, but at a $1,499 starting price ($200 more than before), there are better options — including other Macs.

I tested the iMac M6 in a pretty, pale blue color, with the higher-end 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU (with a dual 16-core neural engine) and 16GB of memory. After recently reviewing a Mac Studio M5 Ultra with 256GB of RAM, I was curious to try a Mac model configured with the least amount of memory possible.

Apple didn't release a new iMac last year, so the biggest change from the 2024 model is an upgrade from the M4 to the M6 processor. The new chip adds two extra cores to both the base and high-end models, with the latter offering up to a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU instead of 10 cores for both as before. Apple says that memory bandwidth is higher as well at 170GB/s max, compared to the previous 120GB/s. The new model also comes with Apple's latest N1 wireless chip, so it now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, compared to Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 on the iMac M4.

Otherwise, the new iMac is the same old iMac. It still comes with a 24-inch 4.5K (4,480 x 2,250) 500-nit IPS display, available with and without a nano-textured coating that reduces glare (a $200 option). The elegant stand still has a tilt but not a height adjustment, and it offers four Thunderbolt 4 ports on the higher-end model and two on the base version. Other features carried over from before include the magnetic power connector, 3.5mm headphone jack and sharp 12-megapixel webcam introduced on the last model.

The iMac is available with the same seven color options as before, including blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver, with accessories (the mouse, keyboard and cables) in matching shades. The colors on the front are subdued, but they're more saturated on the back.

Since the iMac skipped the M5 chip, the M6 model is noticeably quicker than before. Apple claims it's up to 50 percent faster for productivity apps like Microsoft Excel compared to the last model, while offering a similar speed bump for things like photo and video editing.

The M6 chip is particularly proficient for AI, with Apple claiming five times faster on-device performance in LM Studio compared to the M4 model. However, keep in mind that AI models work best with plenty of memory and the iMac only offers 16GB, 24GB or 32GB configurations — tied with the MacBook Air for the least of any Mac product.

In my tests, performance largely lived up to Apple's claims. The iMac M6 scored 4,552 and 20,363 points on Geekbench 6's single- and multi-core CPU tests, around a 20 percent bump from the previous model. It did even better on Geekbench 6 GPU (metal) with a mark of 88,276, more than double the previous model. Cinebench 2024 scores were also up 38 percent on the GPU side and 25 percent/40 percent in single/multi-core tests compared to the iMac M4. Finally, the M6 iMac scored 81,050 on Geekbench AI ML, a significant increase from 50,704 before.

Disk speeds are key for low-memory computers, and fortunately, the iMac M6 didn't disappoint here. Those were more than double the previous model, with 12.4GB/s write and 6.76GB/s read speeds — right up there with the Mac Studio M5 Ultra's pace.

Benchmarks are one thing, but I was keen to test the new iMac for quotidian tasks like content creation, gaming and AI. As a machine for school or corporate work, it's great, with minimal lag and zippy performance for spreadsheets and video calls. It's also nice for entertainment, thanks to the bright and colorful (but too small) display with 4K HDR. The six-speaker setup with two force-canceling woofers and Dolby Atmos support also provides decent sound for an all-in-one (AIO) PC.

For some chores, though, my machine was impeded by its relatively meager RAM allocation. Blackmagic Design's DaVinci Resolve is a great test for creative work, and though the iMac did better than I expected, I saw a few issues. I was able to play back a mix of 4K MP4 files from a DJI drone and 6K RAW Nikon files without any issues. However, after adding effects, extra tracks and completing more edits, I saw some interface lag and playback skipping. For basic TikTok and YouTube editing, though, the iMac M6 performed well for me.

Gaming's not a strong point, though. With Cyberpunk 2077, I saw just 50 fps at 1080p with the default graphics settings, and was only able to achieve 60 fps dialing down the quality. Other games like Resident Evil Biohazard and Baldur's Gate 3 had similar performance issues, with 1080p resolution the maximum possible for playable frame rates. With an extra 8GB of RAM, my colleague Devindra Hardawar saw slightly better performance when gaming on a Mac mini with the same M6 chip.

When it comes to AI work, my machine definitely needed more RAM. I tested it using LM Studio with the quen3.5-9b model that matches well to this Mac. It ran at around 30 tokens per second for translation and other prompts, which isn't amazing for a machine at this price. Due to its small model limitations, it also produced some inaccuracies, so the iMac M6 won't be the AI computer of your dreams unless you upgrade the memory.

In my last iMac review, I said that the 24-inch display was "ample" for most work, but I'm no longer of that mind. With extra speed that makes the iMac more useful for AI and creative work, the display is simply too small and that Apple needs to offer at least a 27-inch screen on future models.

Though its design is getting dated, there's still a lot to like about the new iMac M6. It's a good productivity and entertainment machine, and it can even handle light gaming and creative work. The main problem, for me, though, is that you no longer get enough for your money. The base model starts at $1,499 with 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, but the sweet spot is the version with the 12-core CPU and GPU and 24GB of RAM — more speed and two extra Thunderbolt ports. All of that pushes the price up to $1,899.

Here's the problem: You can purchase a Mac mini with the same M6 chip and 24GB of RAM for $1,099, leaving you $800 to buy a bigger and brighter display with a height adjustment, like LG's 27-inch 5K Ultragear Mini-LED model. Or, you could get a cheaper monitor and spend less.

With that said, if you really want an AIO computer for its simplicity and ease of setup, the iMac is the best one out there. It outperforms Windows models like the Lenovo Yoga AIO 27 for a similar price, particularly in the areas of productivity and content creation. If you don't mind a couple of extra cables, though, the Mac mini with a bigger display is a better option for most people.

#313. Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market

US leader in deploying humanoid robots goes public on the Nasdaq stock exchange.

Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States.

The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor.

“When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. “Because they’re paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.”

Agility is one of many startups attempting to commercialize humanoid robots. But the company has stood out from the competition through its lead in deploying and operating Digit humanoid robots with multiple customers, including the warehouses of logistics company GXO, the South Carolina factory of German automotive manufacturer Schaeffler, and the automotive production lines of Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. As Agility’s very first customer, GXO announced it would expand deployments of Digit robots beyond a warehouse in Georgia to additional facilities in North Carolina and Tennessee.

The filings accompanying Agility’s journey toward becoming a publicly traded company—based on a merger with a special purpose acquisition company—also provide a rare look at the business prospects and potential unit economics of humanoid robots. Most of its startup competitors remain privately held companies that have not been nearly as forthcoming.

Another exception has been China’s humanoid robotics company Unitree, which opened its books when it went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market in August 2026.

Agility described the “illustrative unit economics” for both its “robots-as-a-service” subscription business and an “ownership model,” which would involve corporate clients purchasing robots outright, in an S-4 registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on September 4.

With the subscription model, customers would pay a one-time cost of about $25,000 per robot for delivery and deployment to a work site, along with a recurring monthly fee of $8,500 for software and maintenance.

Customers can also purchase the robot’s hardware outright for a one-time payment of $200,000, along with another one-time cost of $20,000 for delivery and deployment. But that still comes with an annual subscription fee of $36,000 for software and maintenance, or about $3,000 per month.

In exchange for renting or purchasing the robots, customers would get access to the latest Agility robot, known as Digit 5, starting in 2027. The bipedal robot has swappable end-effector “hands,” can lift up to 50-pound loads, and can perform more than 20 hours of work in a 24-hour period with the help of a fast-charging battery system.

The fast-charging battery technology provided by the UK-based company Nyobolt requires just nine minutes to deliver 90 minutes of robot runtime. “We worked with them for well over a year to design the pack that goes in our robot,” Hurst told Ars. “So the battery pack is fully custom and is ours, and we have the exclusive agreement with Nyobolt around using their [battery] chemistry in humanoid robots.”

The Digit 5 also comes with an onboard safety system that enables it to detect humans moving nearby and take appropriate actions, like standing still or squatting to minimize the risk of harm. That could unlock more opportunities to deploy Digit 5 beyond the confines of isolated work cells within warehouses and factories, said Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at Agility, in a previous conversation with Ars.

During a presentation for analysts and investors on October 6, Agility’s chief financial officer, Michael Beer, described the Digit subscription model as allowing customers to replace $200,000 in annual labor costs with $100,000 in annual robot costs, while buying a Digit robot outright could replace $1.1 million in labor costs with about $400,000 in robot costs over five years.

Meanwhile, Agility described its own annual operating costs per robot as being $15,000 to provide the necessary software and maintenance, along with a one-time cost of $15,000 for Agility to initially deploy each robot.

The robotics company also estimated each Digit v5 humanoid robot as initially costing Agility $150,000 based on the bill of materials. Each robot is estimated to have a useful operational lifespan of about five years.

But Agility anticipates that bill of materials cost falling to $75,000 per robot once it ramps up to annual production of 1,000 robots, and eventually $30,000 per robot if the company can produce 10,000 robots per year. The company plans to gradually ramp up production at its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Oregon.

When balancing such business costs versus revenue, Agility anticipates that it could earn about $500,000 per robot on an annual basis through the subscription model, and about $400,000 per robot each year if a customer purchases the Digit robots outright while paying ongoing software and maintenance fees.

The subscription revenue calculations disclosed in Agility’s S-4 filing were based on an unidentified customer’s $300 million order covering 1,000 Digit 5 robots over a three-year subscription contract.

However, such a customer order does not mean Agility is guaranteed to earn $300 million, because the contract requires the robotics company to deliver on certain “contractual milestones, product features and specifications.”

The robotics company’s financial disclosures also bluntly state that “Agility has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future.” In 2025, the company earned just $1.8 million in revenue against $140 million in operating loss, which shows it’s still in the early stages of building a sustainable business.

Agility said it continues to devote “substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot,” while continuing to expand the RoboFab manufacturing facility. On October 21, Agility also announced plans to build a new facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for supporting Digit robot deployments and further developing the robot’s software and AI.

Beyond the challenges of building its own business, Agility’s financial disclosures also cautioned that “competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying rapidly, with well-funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics, among others, actively developing competing humanoid systems.”

Many of those companies have advantages, such as “significantly greater brand recognition, customer relationships, and financial, technical, manufacturing, and other resources,” Agility’s S-4 filing acknowledged. It also listed business risks involving uncertain AI-driven robotic performance in the real world, safety issues in sharing workspaces with human workers, changing regulations, and cybersecurity threats.

Still, Agility co-founder Hurst described a large potential market with “millions of unfilled roles” involving manual tasks that would typically require higher-cost but relatively low-skilled human labor. Within the next year, Hurst expects multiple Agility customers to be sharing videos of the Digit robots “just very boringly doing their work” to the point where “all of the excitement and hype and novelty of humanoids has worn off.”

“It’ll look a bit like the dawn of the automotive market, and different companies will have different niches—some companies will build the Ford F-150 and some companies will build a Mazda Miata,” Hurst told Ars. “There’s going to be a bunch of different niches for multi-purpose human-centric machines like these.”

Although Hurst sees Agility’s path eventually leading to a general-purpose autonomous robot in the future, he has consistently dismissed the idea of any company immediately deploying humanoid robots to riskier and less structured environments, like people’s homes. “Digit 5 is not going to walk into your living room and do dishes and stuff like that,” he said. “Nobody is.”

Whatever happens with Agility’s journey in the coming years, it will be instructive for anyone interested in the broader trajectory of the humanoid robot industry.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#312. 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 First Drive: Big displays meet big V8s

Chevy's new Silverado needs a few updates before it's ready for prime time.

Global fuel prices are spiraling out of control and smaller, more efficient engines are powering more and more cars, but don't tell that to Chevrolet. The new 2027 Silverado 1500 features a pair of new, bigger V8 engines that make more power and torque, delivering better towing and hauling, but sucking down more fuel in the process.

The bigger story, though, is what's going on in the cabin. A wholly new, Android-based infotainment experience with both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay runs across the entire dashboard, powering up to three displays plus a heads-up display above. Add on a fold-out workspace plus integrated 5G connectivity in a cabin bigger than most Manhattan apartments, and you have a potentially excellent mobile workspace.

It even has hands-off driving and a suite of new features and cameras that make towing a cinch. It's a compelling truck in the making, but as I learned after spending a few days wheeling several different trucks across and around Tucson, Arizona, things aren't quite fully baked.

We'll get the numbers out of the way first, since performance figures sell trucks. For 2027, Chevrolet offers four different engines in the Silverado 1500. The smallest and most efficient of the bunch is a 2.7-liter turbocharged engine, which may sound underwhelming in a truck this size. But, with 350 horsepower and 455 pound-feet of torque, it's only lightweight compared with the rest of the lineup.

That now includes a new 5.7-liter V8, replacing the previously available 5.3. Power and torque step up to 402 horsepower and 428 pound-feet. The last gasoline-powered option is also new: a 6.6-liter V8 that delivers 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet. That's the most powerful, but it's actually the 5.7 that enables the 1500's maximum tow rating of 13,700 pounds.

The fourth option is Chevrolet's Duramax diesel, with a 3.0-liter displacement, 305 horsepower and a whopping 495 pound-feet of torque. This is the most fuel-efficient of the bunch, with Chevrolet promising 900 miles out of the 34-gallon tank. This was formerly the economical choice, but the soaring prices of the stuff at the pump these days make this a little less appealing.

Chevrolet has seven trims available for the 1500, with the cheapest, the basic Work Truck trim starting at $41,395. From there, as you add on features like locking differentials, uprated suspension and luxurious interior touches, prices quickly climb. The base price on a top-trim, off-road-focused ZR2 is $79,995 after the $2,795 destination charge.

The new 1500 doesn't look radically different from last year's model, but it has seen some substantial design changes that make it look a little less busy and a little more sophisticated than in years past. It's perhaps not the most exciting-looking truck, but it is at least good-looking, something you couldn't necessarily say about the past few years' worth of Silverado.

Much more substantial changes are inside. For 2027, a 16.3-inch central touchscreen is standard, taking up much of the middle of the dashboard and is conjoined to a second display: a 12.2-inch unit that makes up the digital gauge cluster behind the steering wheel.

That includes services like Disney+, Hulu and YouTube, plus iHeartRadio and Amazon Music. You can even bring your own video thanks to an HDMI input. Combine that with the available three-prong outlet, and if you pack your PlayStation 5 you could get some quality GTA VI time in from the passenger seat.

My biggest disappointment, though, is how little you can do with that display. It's for streaming, and that's about it. To me, the most useful feature of passenger displays is letting your co-driver search for destinations and scroll around the map without taking over the driver's navigation view. You can't do that here, and while the Silverado does have an AI-powered co-driver onboard that can do some of that for you, in my testing it didn't always work.

Chevrolet's new Android-based experience has plenty to be happy about, not least the massive display, which is bright, clear and generally easy to reach. Performance of the interface is also quite good, and I appreciate having Google Maps built right into the truck. It's my preferred way of figuring out which way to get where I'm going, and not having to rely on my phone is a bonus.

That said, it's extra nice to use my phone when I want to. Chevrolet has happily excluded support for both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from most of its EVs, but the new Silverados have thankfully been saved from that misguided decision. Both services work here and wirelessly, even.

That's good, because I didn't love everything going on in the rest of the interface. While the bulk of it is clean and easy, vehicle settings are spread across a few different areas, with many of them hidden behind a quick-access panel accessible only via a tiny icon on the lower-left of the display.

Other frequently used features, like the truck's 360-degree camera view (something you will definitely need for parking), are also accessible via more tiny icons arrayed along the top of the display. Given the size of, well, everything in the new Silverado, I'm not sure why they're so small. Hitting one while on the go is a genuine challenge.

Those cameras aren't just useful for successfully wedging your 5,800-pound, six-plus-foot-long truck into a parking space. Chevrolet puts cameras beneath the truck on its ZR2 model, so you can see whether your rear differential is about to shed its vital fluids upon a rock on the trail.

Cameras are also essential for many of the towing-centric features that make trailering a lot easier than it used to be. You can buy wired, remote cameras to mount on, and even in, whatever you're trailering. The truck can then create a "transparent trailer" mode, enabling you to see what's behind you when you're backing up as if your payload weren't there. You can also get a view inside of the trailer, useful if you have a nervous pony stomping around back there.

The Super Cruise hands-free driving system has also been optimized for towing, and I got a chance to go hands-free on a bumpy, narrow road with a 4,300-pound trailer behind. The system made it easy, keeping the truck perfectly centered without issue.

However, Super Cruise wasn't always perfect. On a later stretch of highway, driving trailer-free in a different Silverado, Super Cruise tried to automatically change lanes right into a motorcycle that was in the midst of passing me. I had to grab the wheel to stop the change. It was a surprising gaffe from a safety system that, in my experience, has been near bulletproof in the past.

So the interface isn't perfect, and Super Cruise isn't either, but those are issues that can hopefully be quickly and easily addressed via a software update. What about the rest of the truck, the parts that won't be so easy to address? I was quite impressed.

I got to sample three out of the four engines, and all proved quite capable for towing and general driving. Yes, the 6.6-liter V8 was strong and had plenty of torque to drive the ZR2 model I tested up and over every obstacle in its way. But honestly, the 5.7 felt very nearly as strong on the road, and I have to imagine for everyday use the four-cylinder will be plenty.

Out on Tucson's highways and byways, the Silverado 1500 was surprisingly pleasant. Its ride quality has just enough of a harsh edge on it to remind you that you're driving a box-frame truck with live axles at either end, but not so punishing that you'll hate your life over every concrete separation joint. It's even reasonably quiet at highway speed, and the interior is so massively roomy on the Crew Cab that you won't have to worry about your kids in the second seat getting in each other's faces.

The new Silverado is an impressive package already, though it'll need a software update or two to reach its full potential. Until then, the inclusion of wireless CarPlay and Android Auto is very appreciated, especially with the dual magnetic Qi chargers. The Super Cruise implementation here clearly still has a few kinks to work out, but otherwise the truck has a lot to offer.

That said, driving something like this is quite a commitment, both in terms of how much space it'll take up in your life and how much it'll drink. While Chevrolet doesn't post fuel economy figures for these trucks, I averaged 16.2 mpg in a 5.7-liter V8-equipped truck. And with that Trail Boss-trim truck coming in at $76,100 after destination with the options you see above, gas won't be the only thing you're paying for.

#311. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#310. Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release

In 2001, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" hit cinemas and took the world by storm. Today, anticipation for the new series is high, but its creator, J.K. Rowling, remains a controversial figure.

On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."

The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

#308. Motorola's new Signature 27 has it all if you can stomach the $1,600 price tag

It has all the bells and whistles (and cameras).

Motorola is patching a hole in its US lineup with a non-folding flagship phone, but the pricing puts this device dangerously close to the company’s expensive tablet-style foldable. The long-rumored Motorola Signature 27 is real, featuring top-of-the-line specs, a super-bright OLED screen, and a ton of cameras. But all this high-end hardware won’t come cheap in the age of AI. Motorola’s new flagship smartphone will run a whopping $1,600 when it arrives later this month.

The Signature 27 is a new take on flagship smartphones from Motorola, leaving behind the middling legacy of the Edge series. However, you’ll still immediately clock this as a Motorola device due to its distinctive use of materials and Pantone colors. The phone is metal, ceramic, and glass, but the backs are textured polycarbonate. The device comes in Coal Smoke (black) or Capulet Olive (green) colors. The former has a “tactical weave” finish inspired by automotive design, and the latter is “textile-inspired.”

This device will include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most powerful mobile chip Qualcomm offers right now. While some smartphones have flirted with 16GB of memory, that’s less common these days. The Signature 27 will have 12GB like Samsung’s base model flagships. However, there’s not going to be an upgrade option for more. You will, however, get a generous 512GB of storage.

The phone is fairly thin in most places, but it tapers outward near the camera module. It’s easy to see why Moto needed a little more space up there with four image sensors. Note: That’s not four cameras. There are three standard cameras: a 50MP primary, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 200MP 3x optical zoom (100x digital zoom). Joining the cameras is an event-based vision sensor (EVS) to power a feature called Action Shot.

The action sensor measures changes in light at a pixel level, which makes it ideal for tracking moving subjects. Action Shot will turn on automatically when the phone detects a lot of movement in the frame, but you can also activate it manually. Motorola’s cameras have long struggled to capture moving subjects clearly, so it’ll be interesting to see if the EVS fixes that.

If you’ve been thinking about a smaller phone, the Signature 27 isn’t for you. This phone sports a sizable 6.8-inch OLED screen with a 120Hz refresh rate. This is a tandem OLED panel, which uses stacked pixels to increase brightness. Moto claims the Signature 27 can hit an impressive 12,000 nits of peak brightness, which is four times higher than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (and the highest of any smartphone). A possible drawback is that tandem OLEDs tend to have a somewhat uneven appearance at low brightness with solid colors, but we haven’t seen the Signature 27 in person yet to say whether or not that’s the case here.

A display like that could really drain your battery, but the Signature 27 has capacity to spare. The 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon cell is the largest of any mainstream smartphone, 1,000 mAh larger than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Motorola estimates it could last two days on a charge, and it won’t take long to refill. With a compatible USB-C charger (not included), the Signature 27 can reach speeds up to 90W. Moto claims up to 12 hours of usage in 12 minutes of charging.

The Motorola Signature 27 will ship with Android 17 and Moto’s Hello UI customizations. The company promises seven years of OS updates, on par with Samsung and Google.

This will be a full Gemini Intelligence device, entitling it to Google’s most expansive list of AI features. Moto says the Signature 27 will get Google’s agentic app control, Create My Widget, Sign-to-Text, and Rambler voice input. However, these features will arrive “in the coming months,” as most of those features are still limited to Pixel phones.

Moto is still offering a parallel set of AI features on its phones. Features like Catch me up (notification summaries) and Pay Attention (meeting notes) are still supported, but the company appears to have dropped the Moto AI branding. Instead, these are all part of Motorola Qira, an AI platform that also connects your Motorola phone to Lenovo computers.

#307. TikTok launches standalone TikTok Shop app (in four markets)

TikTok has spent years making it easier to buy the products that appear in makeup tutorials, cooking videos, and creator recommendations in TikTok Shop. Now, it’s giving shoppers a separate app to open when they're in the mood to spend on a new lip gloss, a milk frother, or another pair of sneakers.

The company has (rather quietly) released a standalone TikTok Shop app in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines on iOS and Android, as social media consultant Matt Navarra first spotted on X. The launch gives TikTok's growing shopping business its own place on a phone's home screen.

According to its Apple App Store listing, the app offers personalized product recommendations, livestreams and short videos showing products in action, checkout, order tracking, and 24/7 customer support. Shoppers are also being offered app-exclusive deals, free shipping promotions, and first-order perks.

The Google Play listing shows more than 50,000 downloads, while the Singapore Apple App Store lists it at No. 71 in the shopping category, with a single five-star rating. Its latest iOS update, version 45.5.5, arrived just 13 hours before publication (at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 5).

The app's Singapore App Store listing names TikTok Pte. Ltd. as its provider, a separate company from TikTok USDS Joint Venture, which operates TikTok in the U.S. The majority-American-owned joint venture handles U.S. data security, recommendation algorithms, and content moderation, while TikTok's global business still manages commercial activities, including e-commerce.

It's unclear whether the standalone shopping app will launch in the U.S. TikTok has not yet responded to Mashable's request for comment.

Giving Shop a dedicated app could help TikTok compete for the moments when someone opens Amazon or Temu intending to browse or buy. Videos and livestreams remain part of the experience, according to the listings, but shopping becomes the reason to open the app in the first place. That fits into a broader expansion Mashable has been following, as TikTok builds more services around the recommendations people encounter on its platform.

Creators can also earn commissions through eligible content, giving a travel recommendation a more direct connection to a reservation.

TikTok's announcement describes a process that takes people from discovering a place in a video to checking availability and booking it. As CEO of TikTok USDS Joint Venture Adam Presser said at the time, the platform is "good for creators, good for local businesses, and good for communities."

And more recently, TikTok launched Must Eat, TikTok's restaurant guide for the areas around New York City, Los Angeles, and the San Francisco Bay Area. Built from more than 40 million posts, reviews, and comments, it organizes food recommendations into searchable lists, with OpenTable reservations available for select restaurants. A video of a particularly good dinner can influence choosing and booking a future reservation.

TikTok has also been experimenting with giving specific kinds of entertainment their own apps. Its PineDrama service, launched earlier this year, puts short dramas into a separate app with personalized recommendations and tools for browsing series and episodes.

Taken together, those products suggest TikTok sees room to build entire services around habits that started in the feed. The standalone Shop app puts that idea to another test, asking whether people who discover products on TikTok will also choose it when shopping is what they came to do.

#306. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#305. Instagram's Edits is now on desktop as a Mac app

Meta's CapCut competitor already has more than 50 million users.

Instagram's video editing app Edits now has its own Mac version. According to Meta, the desktop experience will allow creators to tackle more "ambitious projects" that aren't necessarily suited for the mobile version.

Edits on desktop has a similar setup to the phone version. Creators can stitch together multiple clips and audio tracks, along with visual effects and music from its audio library. It takes advantage of the increased screen real estate to offer the kind of fine-tuned control that's difficult to achieve with a mobile interface.

"Our new desktop editor brings a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for dynamic transitions, and precise audio waveforms for beat-accurate cuts," Meta explains in a blog post. "Splitting, cutting, and trimming are all easier, and color wheels, log conversions, and curves give your videos a finished grade." The app also supports dedicated keyboard shortcuts and custom fonts.

And, like the mobile version of the app, Edits users can export their finished product without a watermark and publish videos directly to Instagram without leaving the app.

Meta released Edits early last year to compete with ByteDance's CapCut, which is still the go-to editing app for many TikTok creators. But Meta's video editor has gained momentum. During Meta's most recent earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that Edits has more than 50 million active users.

The company says that it's already working on additional features for the desktop software, including the ability to move between the desktop and mobile app while editing the same project.
